front: What is the kube-apiserver and why is it central?
back: The single front door to the cluster. Every request (kubectl, internal components, webhooks) flows through it; it validates requests and persists state to etcd. Components never talk to each other directly — they all go through the API server (hub-and-spoke).
source: Kubernetes Foundations — Understanding Kubernetes architecture

front: What does etcd store and why is backing it up a dedicated exam competency?
back: etcd is a distributed key-value store holding the entire cluster state (every pod, service, configmap, secret) — the single source of truth. Only the API server talks to it. Lose etcd without a backup and you lose the cluster.
source: Kubernetes Foundations — Understanding Kubernetes architecture

front: What is the difference between the kube-scheduler and the kube-controller-manager?
back: The scheduler watches for unscheduled pods and picks a node (it places, it does not run). The controller-manager runs reconciliation loops (deployment, replicaset, node controllers) comparing desired vs actual state and closing the gap — the self-healing engine.
source: Kubernetes Foundations — Understanding Kubernetes architecture

front: What are the three node components and their roles?
back: kubelet (node agent that pulls pod specs from the API server and runs containers via the CRI, watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests for static pods); kube-proxy (programs iptables/IPVS rules for service VIPs, runs as a DaemonSet); container runtime (containerd — pulls images and runs containers).
source: Kubernetes Foundations — Understanding Kubernetes architecture

front: What is a static pod and where do the control plane static pods live?
back: A static pod is run directly by the kubelet from a YAML file on disk (no scheduler or deployment). The four control plane manifests live in /etc/kubernetes/manifests (kube-apiserver.yaml, etcd.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml). Edit one and the kubelet restarts that pod automatically.
source: Kubernetes Foundations — Contrasting nodes and pods

front: Define CRI, CNI, and CSI.
back: CRI (Container Runtime Interface): how the kubelet talks to the runtime via gRPC (containerd, CRI-O). CNI (Container Network Interface): how pods get IPs and pod-to-pod routing (Calico, Flannel, Cilium). CSI (Container Storage Interface): how persistent storage is provisioned/attached via vendor drivers.
source: Kubernetes Foundations — Kubernetes extension interfaces

front: A container won't start, a pod has no IP, and a PV is stuck Pending. Which interface owns each?
back: Container won't start → CRI/runtime. Pod has no IP → CNI. PersistentVolume stuck Pending → CSI/StorageClass. Naming the interface narrows the troubleshooting search space instantly.
source: Kubernetes Foundations — Kubernetes extension interfaces

front: Why must swap be disabled before kubeadm init?
back: The kubelet refuses to run with swap enabled because the scheduler needs accurate, deterministic memory accounting. Disable with 'swapoff -a' and remove the swap line from /etc/fstab so it stays off after reboot. Verify with 'swapon --show' (empty output).
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — kubeadm prerequisites

front: Which two kernel modules and three sysctl values does kubeadm require, and why?
back: Modules: overlay (OverlayFS for containerd image layers) and br_netfilter (makes bridged L2 traffic visible to iptables). sysctls: net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 (L3 forwarding so pods route across nodes), net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 and -ip6tables=1 (bridged traffic visible to iptables). All sysctls are 0 on stock Ubuntu.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Kernel modules and sysctl

front: Pods on different nodes can't reach each other but each has an IP. What's the first thing to check?
back: Check 'sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables' on every node — it must be 1. A value of 0 is a silent failure: pods get IPs and kubeadm preflight can pass, but cross-node traffic times out with no obvious error.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Verifying kernel modules and sysctl

front: What is the #1 cause of kubeadm init failures involving containerd?
back: A cgroup driver mismatch. containerd ships with SystemdCgroup = false but the kubelet uses the systemd cgroup driver. Set SystemdCgroup = true in /etc/containerd/config.toml and restart containerd. A mismatch makes pods crash-loop while logs point at the wrong layer.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — containerd and the CRI

front: Why pin and 'apt-mark hold' kubeadm, kubelet, and kubectl?
back: All three must run the same minor version on every node — version skew breaks the join. 'apt-mark hold' stops a routine 'apt upgrade' from silently bumping the version and corrupting your upgrade plan. Install them together at one version on every node.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Pinning Kubernetes versions

front: Which kubeadm init flag most often breaks clusters, and what must it match?
back: --pod-network-cidr. It must match what your CNI expects (Calico default 192.168.0.0/16, Flannel 10.244.0.0/16). A mismatch is a silent failure: pods get IPs but can't route across nodes, with no clean error message.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — kubeadm init flags that matter

front: What does the --control-plane-endpoint flag do and why set it on a single-node init?
back: It declares a DNS name in front of the API server, written into every certificate's SAN list at issuance. Setting it now (even pointing to one IP) makes future HA a config change instead of a certificate reissue — later it can resolve to a load balancer in front of multiple control plane nodes.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — kubeadm init flags that matter

front: What does --upload-certs do during kubeadm init?
back: It stores the control plane TLS certificates in a Secret in kube-system with a 2-hour TTL, so additional control plane nodes can join later without manually SCP-ing certificates between hosts.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Creating the init manifest

front: After kubeadm init, kubectl returns 'connection refused'. How do you fix it?
back: admin.conf is root-only. Copy it to your user: mkdir -p $HOME/.kube; sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config; sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config. Now kubectl works without sudo.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Managing kubeconfig

front: After kubeadm init the nodes are NotReady and CoreDNS is Pending. Is this a failure?
back: No — it's expected and correct. The kubelet won't mark a node Ready until a CNI plug-in can assign pod IPs, and CoreDNS needs a pod IP to start. kube-proxy uses host networking so it runs anyway. Installing the CNI flips nodes to Ready in ~30 seconds.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — From init to ready

front: How does the kubeadm join bootstrap token secure two-way verification?
back: The bootstrap token (format: 6-char id . 16-char secret, 24-hour TTL) authenticates the worker to the API server. The --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash (SHA-256 of the CA cert) lets the worker confirm it's talking to the genuine control plane, preventing a man-in-the-middle.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Bootstrap tokens and join workflow

front: You lost the join command from the kubeadm init output. How do you regenerate it?
back: Run 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command' on the control plane. It emits a complete, ready-to-paste join command with a fresh token and the correct CA cert hash.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Bootstrap tokens and join workflow

front: Why is Calico the recommended CNI for CKA practice over Flannel?
back: Calico implements the NetworkPolicy API (tested in the Services & Networking domain), installs cleanly with kubeadm, and is the most widely deployed CNI in self-managed production. Flannel is simpler but has no NetworkPolicy, so it can't cover half that domain.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Comparing CNI plugins

front: What three things does a Kubernetes context bundle?
back: A cluster (API server endpoint + CA cert), a user (credentials/identity), and a default namespace. 'kubectl config use-context <name>' switches; 'kubectl config current-context' verifies.
source: Kubernetes Foundations — Context management

front: Why do 'kubectl config' commands succeed even when the cluster is unreachable?
back: kubectl config only reads/writes your local kubeconfig file (~/.kube/config), not the API server. That's why context switching is your safe first command after each exam question, before any work hits the cluster.
source: Kubernetes Foundations — When to use YAML instead of imperative

front: Is Kubernetes RBAC additive or subtractive, and what happens with no matching binding?
back: Purely additive — there are no deny rules. If a subject isn't explicitly granted a permission via a binding, the API server returns 403 Forbidden (secure by default).
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — The foundation of RBAC

front: When do you use a Role vs a ClusterRole?
back: A Role is namespaced — use it when a task names a specific namespace. A ClusterRole is cluster-wide — use it for cluster-scoped resources (nodes, persistent volumes, namespaces) or as a reusable permission template across namespaces.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Cluster-wide permissions

front: What is the difference between a RoleBinding and a ClusterRoleBinding?
back: A RoleBinding grants permissions within a single namespace (and can bind either a Role or a ClusterRole). A ClusterRoleBinding grants a ClusterRole's permissions across the entire cluster. Binding a ClusterRole via a RoleBinding scopes those permissions to just that namespace (hybrid/DRY pattern).
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Cluster-wide permissions

front: What three parts make up an RBAC rule?
back: apiGroups ("" for core resources like pods/services, 'apps' for deployments), resources (pods, configmaps...), and verbs (get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete). Note: get retrieves one object; list retrieves all of a type.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — The foundation of RBAC

front: How do you verify whether a service account can delete pods in the default namespace?
back: kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:<sa-name> -n default. It sends a SubjectAccessReview to the API server. Use --list to see all effective permissions for a subject.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Checking API access with can-i

front: Which kubectl verbosity level is the sweet spot for debugging an RBAC 403, and what does it show?
back: -v=8. It prints the raw HTTP request (curl equivalent), request headers including the authorization bearer token, and the response body. -v=6 shows the URL and HTTP status code (e.g., 403 Forbidden, 404 NotFound).
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Accessing resources with kubectl -v

front: What three built-in ClusterRoles should you know, plus the break-glass one?
back: view (read-only), edit (read/write workloads), admin (full namespace control). cluster-admin grants everything on every resource — use only for break-glass emergencies, never everyday access.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Security — Introducing Authentication and RBAC

front: How does a service account authenticate to the API server, and how do you stop a pod from getting a token?
back: The API server injects a JWT token into the pod's filesystem (/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/). For workloads that don't call the API, set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the Pod spec or the ServiceAccount — no token means no API access even if the container is compromised.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Security — Understanding End-user Authentication

front: Why must control plane (etcd) nodes use an odd number, and what is quorum?
back: etcd uses the Raft consensus protocol needing a majority to decide. Quorum = N/2 + 1. Odd numbers (3, 5, 7) prevent split-brain and maximize fault tolerance. A 3-node control plane survives losing 1 node; a 2-node cluster is worse than 1 because losing either node loses quorum.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Introduction to high availability

front: Contrast stacked etcd vs external etcd topologies.
back: Stacked: each control plane node runs its own local etcd as a static pod (cheaper, simpler, kubeadm manages membership — common for medium clusters). External: etcd runs on dedicated hosts decoupled from the API servers (more hardware/complexity, highest stability, scale API and etcd independently — for very large clusters).
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Introduction to high availability

front: What roles do HAProxy and Keepalived play in an HA control plane?
back: HAProxy load-balances traffic (round-robin) across the multiple API servers on port 6443, actively health-checking each. Keepalived provides a virtual IP that floats to a surviving load balancer if one fails, keeping the API endpoint reachable. Point --control-plane-endpoint at this stable address.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Demo: Setting up the load balancer

front: Write the etcdctl command to take a snapshot, including the required credentials.
back: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key. etcd requires full TLS auth, so all three (cacert, cert, key) plus the endpoint are mandatory.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Disaster recovery

front: What is the correct ordered workflow to restore an etcd snapshot?
back: 1) Stop the control plane by moving etcd.yaml and kube-apiserver.yaml out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests. 2) etcdctl snapshot restore --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored (a NEW empty directory, never the live one). 3) Edit etcd.yaml so the etcd-data hostPath points to the restored directory. 4) Move the manifests back. 5) Verify with kubectl get nodes and kubectl get pods -A.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Disaster recovery

front: Why does HA NOT protect you from an accidental 'kubectl delete namespace production'?
back: HA protects against infrastructure failure, not human failure. An HA control plane faithfully replicates the deletion to every node in milliseconds. The defense against accidental deletion is an etcd snapshot (point-in-time backup) you can restore from.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Disaster recovery

front: What is the correct order and one-version rule for upgrading a kubeadm cluster?
back: Upgrade control plane first, then worker nodes, one minor version at a time (never skip versions). On the first control plane node: 'kubeadm upgrade plan' then 'kubeadm upgrade apply v1.X.0'. On other control planes and workers: 'kubeadm upgrade node'. Always drain a node before upgrading its kubelet and uncordon after.
source: Kubernetes docs — Upgrading kubeadm clusters

front: In Helm, what is the difference between a chart and a release?
back: A chart is the package (Chart.yaml metadata, templates/ manifests, values.yaml variables). A release is a specific running instance of that chart in a cluster. Helm tracks release history, enabling 'helm rollback <release> <revision>' to a known-good state.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Templating with Helm

front: How does Kustomize differ from Helm, and how is it invoked?
back: Kustomize is template-less: a base holds plain manifests, and overlays patch only the differences via strategic merge patch (no templating language). It's built into kubectl: 'kubectl apply -k overlays/dev' or 'kubectl kustomize overlays/dev' to preview. Helm uses Go templates, variables, and tracks releases with rollback.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Layering with Kustomize

front: What is a CRD versus an operator?
back: A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) extends the Kubernetes API with a new object type — it's passive data stored in etcd that becomes manageable via kubectl and RBAC. An operator is a custom controller that watches those CRDs and runs the control loop (observe, compare to desired state, act) to automate day-2 operations like backups and upgrades.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — CRDs and the operator pattern

front: How do you quickly generate a correct deployment YAML without writing it by hand?
back: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml, then edit the fields imperative can't express and 'kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml'. dry-run=client builds the manifest locally without touching the API server, producing a 100% syntactically correct starting point.
source: Working with Your Cluster — Working with Manifests and dry-run

front: What is the standard troubleshooting diagnostic ladder for a failing node or pod?
back: kubectl get (identify the failed resource) → kubectl describe (the why, e.g., NetworkPluginNotReady) → kubectl logs → events → journalctl -u kubelet (host-level) → crictl ps/info (runtime). Most exam questions resolve at describe or events.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Troubleshooting with the diagnostic ladder
